en: In the beginning, this universe was indeed the Self alone; there was nothing else whatsoever that blinked. He thought: "Shall I now create the worlds? (1.1.1)

He created these worlds: Ambhas, Marīcis, Mara, and Āpas. Ambhas is that which is beyond the sky; the sky is its support. The intermediate space is Marīcis; the earth is Mara; and those which are below are the Āpas. 1.1.2.
He thought: "Now these worlds exist; let me create the guardians of the worlds. He drew forth a person from the waters alone and gave him form. 1.1.3.

He brooded over that [unformed body]. As it was brooded over, its mouth burst forth like an egg; from the mouth came speech, and from speech, fire. The two nostrils burst forth; from the nostrils came breath (*prāṇa*), and from breath, wind. The two eyes burst forth; from the eyes came sight, and from sight, the sun. The two ears burst forth; from the ears came hearing, and from hearing, the quarters of space. The skin burst forth; from the skin came body hair, and from the body hair, plants and trees. The heart burst forth; from the heart came the mind (*manas*), and from the mind, the moon. The navel burst forth; from the navel came the downward breath (*apāna*), and from the downward breath, death. The male organ burst forth; from the male organ came semen, and from semen, water. (1.1.4)
Thus ends the first section.
These deities, having been created, fell into this great ocean; he afflicted them with hunger and thirst. They said to him, "Find for us an abode in which, being established, we may eat food. (1.2.1)
He brought a cow for them; they said, "This is indeed not enough for us. He brought a horse for them; they said, "This is indeed not enough for us. (1.2.2)
From them he brought forth a person; they said, "Ah, well done! For a person is indeed well done. He said to them, "Enter according to your respective abodes. 1.2.3.

Agni, having become speech, entered the mouth; Vāyu, having become breath, entered the nostrils; Āditya, having become sight, entered the eyes; the Quarters, having become hearing, entered the ears; the herbs and trees, having become body hair, entered the skin; the Moon, having become mind, entered the heart; Death, having become the out-breath, entered the navel; and the Waters, having become semen, entered the generative organ. 1.2.4.

Hunger and thirst said to him, "Take us into account. He replied to them, "I shall give you a share in these very deities; I shall make you partners in them. Therefore, for whichever deity the oblation is taken, hunger and thirst become partners in it. 1.2.5.
Thus ends the second section.
He considered: "Now here are these worlds and the guardians of the worlds; let me create food for them. 1.3.1.
He brooded over the waters; from those waters, thus brooded upon, a form was born. That which was born as form was indeed food. 1.3.2.

Once it was created, it sought to flee away; he tried to seize it with speech, but he was not able to grasp it with speech. Had he been able to grasp it with speech, one would have been satisfied by merely uttering food. 1.3.3.
He sought to grasp it with breath; he was not able to grasp it with breath. For had he grasped it with breath, one would have been satisfied by merely breathing toward food. 1.3.4.
He sought to grasp it with the eye; he was not able to grasp it with the eye. Had he been able to grasp it with the eye, one would have been satisfied merely by seeing food. 1.3.5.
He desired to grasp it with the ear, but he was not able to grasp it with the ear. Had he grasped it with the ear, one would have been satisfied by merely hearing food. 1.3.6.
He sought to grasp it with the skin, but he was not able to grasp it with the skin. Had he grasped it with the skin, he would have been satisfied merely by touching food. 1.3.7.
He sought to grasp it with the mind, but he was not able to grasp it with the mind. Had he been able to grasp it with the mind, one would have obtained food merely by thinking of it. 1.3.8.
He sought to grasp it with his penis; he was not able to grasp it with his penis. Had he grasped it with his penis, he would have been released from food and would have perished. 1.3.9.
He sought to grasp it with the out-breath; he swallowed it. This very wind is the seizer of food; for this wind is indeed the life-sustainer of food. 1.3.10.

He considered: "How indeed might this be without me? He considered: "By which way shall I enter? He considered: "If there is speaking by speech, if there is breathing out by breath, if there is seeing by the eye, if there is hearing by the ear, if there is touching by the skin, if there is thinking by the mind, if there is breathing in by the downward breath, if there is emitting by the organ of generation—then who am I?

He pierced this very boundary and entered through that door. This is the door named "The Piercing" (vidṛti), and this is the "Blissful Place" (nāndana). It has three dwelling places, three states of sleep: "This is a dwelling place, this is a dwelling place, this is a dwelling place.
Once born, he looked upon all beings, thinking, "What else here could I possibly speak? He beheld this very Person as the most pervasive Brahman, saying, "I have seen this! || 1.3.13 ||

Therefore, he is named Indra; for indeed, his name is "Idandra. Although he is Idandra, they call him "Indra" cryptically. For the gods, as it were, love the cryptic; for the gods, as it were, love the cryptic. 1.3.14.
Thus ends the third section.
Thus ends the first chapter.

In truth, this embryo first exists within a man as this semen. Having been produced as a vital essence from all his limbs, he bears himself within his own self. When he pours it into a woman, then he causes it to be born. That is his first birth. (2.1)

Thus, this self of his is assigned to meritorious deeds. Then, this other self of his—having accomplished what was to be done and having reached the end of its term—departs. As soon as he departs from here, he is born again; that is his third birth. 2.4.
This was said by the Seer:
"While still in the womb, I indeed knew all these generations of the gods;
a hundred iron fortresses guarded me, and then, like a hawk, I flew forth with speed. Thus it is said.

While still lying within the womb, Vāmadeva spoke thus: "Knowing this, upon departing upwards from the breaking up of this body, having attained all desires in that heavenly world, he became immortal—he became immortal. (2.5–2.6)
Thus ends the second chapter.

"What is this self that we worship? Which one is that self: that by which one sees, or that by which one hears, or that by which one smells odors, or that by which one articulates speech, or that by which one discerns what is sweet and what is not sweet? (3.1)

That which is this heart and mind—this is perception, discernment, understanding, wisdom, insight, fortitude, thought, intention, impulse, memory, volition, purpose, life-force, desire, and control. All these are indeed names for understanding. 3.2.

This is Brahman; this is Indra; this is Prajāpati; these are all the gods; and these are the five great elements—earth, wind, space, water, and light. These are like seeds mixed with small particles, some born from eggs, some born from wombs, some born from sweat, and some born from sprouts; horses, cows, humans, elephants, and whatever else exists here that has breath—whether moving or flying, or whatever is stationary—all that has consciousness as its guide, is established in consciousness. Consciousness is the eye of the world; consciousness is the foundation; consciousness is Brahman. 3.3.157.
Having departed from this world by means of this intelligent self, he attained all desires in that heavenly world and became immortal—he became immortal. 3.4.
Thus ends the third chapter.
Thus ends the Aitareya Upaniṣad.
